title: Strings and Dictionaries
description: Work with text using string methods and f-strings, and store labelled data in dictionaries.

subLevels.title: String methods
subLevels.summary: Change case, clean, search, split and join text.

blocks.text: Like lists, strings have methods you call with a dot. upper() and lower() change the case.

explanation: upper() gives back a new string in capitals.
The original name is not changed — strings can't be changed in place.

blocks.text: String methods return a NEW string. Store it if you want to keep it.
strip() removes spaces from the start and end. Very useful for user input.

explanation: len() works on strings too and counts characters, including spaces.
After strip() only the 3 letters are left.

blocks.code:
text = "I like tea"
print(text.replace("tea", "coffee"))
print(text.startswith("I"))
print(text.count("e"))
explanation: replace(old, new) swaps every match.
startswith() answers True or False.
count() counts how many times the text appears.

blocks.text: split() breaks a string into a list. join() glues a list of strings back together.

explanation: split(",") cuts the text at every comma.
" & ".join(...) puts " & " between the items.

pages.title: Strings are like lists of letters

blocks.text: You can index a string and loop over its letters, just like a list.

blocks.code:
word = "python"
print(word[0])
print(word[-1])
print(len(word))
for letter in "hi":
    print(letter)

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Calling name.upper() on its own line and expecting name to change. Write name = name.upper() to keep the result.

questions.explanation: upper() turns every letter into a capital, not just the first one.
strip() removes the spaces at both ends, leaving "hi", which has 2 characters. len() gives a number, not the text.
split("-") cuts at each dash and throws the dashes away, giving a list of three strings.

questions.prompt: Why does this still print ravi?
options: Strings must use single quotes for upper()
upper() returns a new string, and the result was never stored
questions.explanation: Strings never change in place. Writing name = name.upper() keeps the capital version.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so the result is "a-b".
questions.explanation: join() glues list items together with the string in front of the dot between them. split() does the opposite.
b-a-n-a-n-a has three a's. 6 is the length of the whole word.

subLevels.title: f-strings and formatting
subLevels.summary: Round numbers and line up columns neatly.

blocks.text: You met f-strings in 1.4. Anything inside { } is worked out first — even a calculation.

blocks.code:
item = "pen"
price = 12
qty = 3
print(f"{qty} x {item} = {price * qty}")

blocks.text: Add :.2f after a value to show exactly 2 decimal places. The number is rounded.

explanation: :.2f means "float with 2 decimals".
The value itself is not changed — only how it is shown.

blocks.text: Add :<8 to left-align a value in 8 spaces, or :>6 to right-align it in 6. This makes neat tables.

explanation: < means left-align, > means right-align.
The number is the width in characters.
Inside a double-quoted f-string, use single quotes for text like 'Item'.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Forgetting the f. print("Hi {name}") prints the braces literally: Hi {name}.
f"{value:.2f}" rounds. f"{value:>6}" lines things up.

questions.explanation: :.2f rounds to 2 decimal places. The third decimal is 1, so it rounds down to 3.14.
Without the f in front of the quotes it's a normal string, so the braces are printed as they are.

options: Right-aligns x in a space 5 characters wide
questions.explanation: > means right-align and 5 is the width. Decimal places use a dot, like :.5f.
Each { } is replaced by its value, and {a + b} is calculated as 9 because a and b are numbers.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank to show 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: :.2f means 2 decimal places. :2f would set a width of 2 instead, which doesn't round anything.

subLevels.title: Dictionaries
subLevels.summary: Store values under labels called keys.

blocks.text: A dictionary stores pairs of key: value inside curly braces { }. You look values up by their key instead of by a position number.

explanation: "name", "age" and "city" are the keys.
student["name"] gives the value stored under "name".
Assigning to a new key adds it.
Assigning to an existing key replaces its value.

blocks.text: Keys are unique. One key, one value.
get() looks up a key but doesn't crash if it's missing. You can give a fallback value.

explanation: "juice" isn't a key, so get() returns None.
get("juice", 0) returns 0 instead.

blocks.code:
ages = {"Asha": 21, "Ravi": 19}
print("Ravi" in ages)
removed = ages.pop("Ravi")
print(removed)
print(len(ages))
explanation: in checks the keys.
pop(key) removes the pair and gives back its value.
len() counts the pairs.

blocks.text: A classic use: count how often each thing appears.

explanation: counts.get(v, 0) is the count so far (0 the first time).
Adding 1 and storing it updates the count.
Square brackets need the key to exist.
Python stops with a KeyError.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Using d[key] for a key that might be missing. Check with in first, or use d.get(key, default).

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Keys are case-sensitive: "Tea" and "tea" are different keys.

questions.explanation: d["b"] looks up the value stored under the key "b", which is 2 — not the key itself.
Keys are unique, so assigning to "x" again replaces the old value.
"milk" is missing, so get() returns the fallback 0. Without a fallback it would return None.

questions.prompt: In a dictionary, what is a key?
options: The label you use to look up a value
The position number of a value
A password that locks the dictionary
questions.explanation: Dictionaries are looked up by key, not by position like lists.

questions.prompt: Why does this raise a KeyError?
questions.explanation: The only key is "pen" in lowercase. Lookups use square brackets, and values can be any type.
Adding "b" makes two key-value pairs, and len() counts pairs.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank to count words safely.
questions.explanation: get(word, 0) returns the current count, or 0 if the word is new. pop would remove the entry.

options: Each key appears only once in a dictionary
All values must be the same type
A dictionary can't be changed after it's created
questions.explanation: Assigning to an existing key replaces its value. Values can be any type, and dictionaries can be changed.

subLevels.title: Looping over dictionaries
subLevels.summary: Visit keys, values and pairs with for loops.

blocks.text: A for loop over a dictionary gives you its keys, in the order they were added.
values() gives just the values. items() gives each key together with its value, so you can use two loop variables. list() turns the result into a normal list for printing.

blocks.output:
['tea', 'coffee', 'juice']
[15, 25, 30]
tea costs 15
coffee costs 25
juice costs 30
explanation: for item, price in ... takes each pair apart into two variables.
This is the most common way to loop over a dictionary.

blocks.code:
sales = {"Mon": 120, "Tue": 90, "Wed": 150}
total = 0
best_day = ""
best = 0
for day, amount in sales.items():
    total += amount
    if amount > best:
        best = amount
        best_day = day
print(f"Total: {total}")
print(f"Best day: {best_day} ({best})")
explanation: total adds every amount.
best remembers the biggest amount seen so far, and best_day its key.

blocks.text: sum(d.values()), max(d.values()) and len(d) also work on dictionaries.

blocks.output: ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)
explanation: Looping over ages gives only the keys, like "Asha".
Python can't split one string into name and age.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Using two loop variables without .items(). Write for name, age in ages.items():

items: for k, v in d.items() — both

questions.explanation: Looping over a dictionary gives its keys. To get values you need .values() or .items().
items() gives each pair and the two variables take it apart, so print shows key and value with a space.
values() gives 2 and 5, and sum() adds them. Keys are not added.

options: Each key together with its value, as pairs
questions.explanation: items() gives key-value pairs. Only values is .values(), and the count is len(d).

questions.prompt: This raises a ValueError. How do you fix it?
options: Loop over marks.items() instead of marks
Put the loop inside a function
questions.explanation: Looping over marks gives only keys, so there's nothing to put in mark. items() gives the pairs.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank to print only the values.
questions.explanation: values() gives just the values. items() would give pairs, and keys() the labels.
